newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds sees $600 million ln first payment under accord.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds sees $600 million ln first payment under accord.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. said Tuesday it expects its initial payment under a recently reached tobacco accord will be $600 million, surprising analysts who thought the number would be much higher.

Analysts had expected RJR Nabisco Holdings' R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. would have to pay a much bigger share of the initial $10 billion payment outlined in the landmark settlement reached Friday with cigarette companies.
"We did not expect it to be this low," said Salomon Brothers analyst Diana Temple. She said some thought RJR Nabisco would have to pony up $2.5 billion for the initial payment.
Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc. analyst Allan Kaplan called the estimate, made in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "a shocker."
RJR said in the filing that it believed implementing the tobacco agreement would "increase the costs and reduce the consumption of (R.J. Reynolds)" tobacco products in the United States.
The company warned this "could have a significant negative effect on the business of (R.J. Reynolds) and the stated financial position" of RJR Nabisco Inc. and the tobacco unit.
Philip Morris Cos. Inc. also filed with the SEC but did not estimate what its portion of the payment would be. Analyst estimates of its share range from $6.7 billion to $7 billion.
Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, the parent of the No. 3 U.S. cigarette maker, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., will pay an estimated $1.7 billion, sources said.
The balance of the $10 billion will come from Loews Corp., the parent of Lorillard Tobacco Co., and smokeless tobacco king UST Inc.
The agreement would require cigarette companies to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate states and smokers and to fund programmes to help people quit smoking.
Of that total, tobacco companies would be required to make an initial $10 billion payment under the agreement and multibillion-dollar annual payments thereafter.

The deal also sets goals of reducing teen smoking by 42 percent in five years, 58 percent in seven years and 67 percent in 10 years or cigarette companies would be penalised by as much as $2 billion a year.

Despite the uncertainties the tobacco giant says it may face if the tobacco accord is finalised, RJR said the proposals contemplated by the agreement "offer a measure of relief from certain litigation that could otherwise materially affect the results of operations or cash flows."
